paragraphs: He said: When the discourse on the obligation of binding-oneself to obedience to God has come before us, I saw that I should follow that with what is most emphasized of matters upon the one obedient to God (exalted be He) — namely, reliance upon Him in all his affairs, on account of what is in this of abundant benefits in religion and in worldly life.

As for its benefit in his religion: among them is the repose of his soul and the leaning of his heart upon his Creator (exalted be He), in accordance with what is incumbent on the slave by way of reliance on his Master. For if he does not rely on God, he will rely on something other than Him. And whoever has relied on something other than God — God turns His care from him and entrusts him to the one upon whom he has leaned. He becomes of the rank of the one of whom it was said: "For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken Me, the fountain of living waters, to hew out for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns that hold no water" (Jeremiah 2:13); and He said: "And they exchanged their Glory for the form of an ox eating grass" (Psalms 106:20). And Scripture said: "Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and whose trust is the Lord" (Jeremiah 17:7); and: "Happy is the man who has made the Lord his trust, and has not turned to the proud and to those swerving with falsehood" (Psalms 40:5); and: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, and from the Lord his heart turns aside" (Jeremiah 17:5).

If he relies on his subtlety, his contrivance, the strength of his body, and his exertion — God entrusts him to himself; his striving is disappointed, his strength weakened, and his contrivance falls short of attaining what he seeks, as Scripture said: "He catches the wise in their craftiness" (Job 5:13); and He said: "I returned and saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor yet bread to the wise, nor riches to the discerning, nor favor to those who know" (Ecclesiastes 9:11); and He said: "The young lions go without and starve, but those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing" (Psalms 34:11).

If he relies on the abundance of his wealth, it is taken from him and he remains without it, as Scripture said: "The rich man lies down, but is not gathered; he opens his eyes, and he is not" (Job 27:19); and He said: "Do not weary yourself to be rich; cease from your understanding. When you cast your eyes upon it, it is not" (Proverbs 23:4–5); and He said: "In the midst of his days he shall leave it" (Jeremiah 17:11). Or he is denied benefit from it, as the Wise One said: "Yet God does not give him power to eat from it" (Ecclesiastes 6:2); so it remains as a deposit with him, kept by him from misfortunes until it passes to the one who is its rightful owner and deserves it, as the Friend said: "And to the sinner He gives the business of gathering and amassing — to give to the one who is good before God" (Ecclesiastes 2:26); and He said: "He prepares it, and the righteous puts it on, and the silver the innocent shall apportion" (Job 27:17). And often the wealth itself is the cause of his perishing and the destruction of his soul, as He said: "There is a grievous evil I have seen under the sun: wealth kept by its owner to his harm" (Ecclesiastes 5:12).

Among them, too: that the one who relies on God is borne by his reliance on Him to abandon the worship of any other than Him, and to cut off his hope from created beings — so that he does not abase himself before them, nor flatter them, nor join with them in other than the obedience to God, nor be in awe of their authority, nor terrified at their opposition. Rather he strips himself of the garment of their gifts and the burden of thanks for them and the obligation of recompensing them. If they admonish him, he does not regard their admonition; if they reproach him, he is not abashed before them; nor does he allow what is false in their eyes to be made attractive to himself — as the Prophet said: "And the Lord God will help me; therefore I have not been confounded; therefore I have set my face like flint, and I knew that I would not be put to shame" (Isaiah 50:7); and He said: "Do not fear them and do not be afraid of their words" (Ezekiel 2:6); and: "Do not be afraid of their words, and do not be dismayed at their faces" (Ezekiel 2:6); and: "Do not fear before them" (Jeremiah 1:8); and: "Like adamant harder than flint I have made your forehead; do not fear them, and do not be dismayed at their faces" (Ezekiel 3:9).

Among them, too: that the one who relies on God is borne by his reliance to free his mind from the affairs of this world and to purify his soul in the works of obedience. He resembles, in the repose of his soul, the ease of his mind, and the slightness of his preoccupation with the affairs of this world — even more than the master of alchemy who has reached its true reality by knowledge and practice. And if his reliance on God is strong, he surpasses him in ten things.

**The first** — the master of alchemy is in need of specific causes without which nothing is completed for him; and he does not find them at every time and in every place. The one who relies on God has his sustenance secured by means of any cause among the causes of the world, as Scripture said: "That He might make you know that not by bread alone shall the human being live, but by everything that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord shall the human being live" (Deuteronomy 8:3). The causes are not impossible for him at any time or in any place, as you have learned from the story of Elijah with the ravens, and the widow woman, and the cake of coals and the cruse of water (1 Kings 17); and the story of Obadiah with the prophets, of whom He said: "And I hid a hundred men of the prophets of the Lord by fifty in a cave, and sustained them with bread and water" (1 Kings 18:13). And He said: "The young lions go without and starve, but those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing" (Psalms 34:11); and He said: "Fear the Lord, you His holy ones, for those who fear Him have no want" (Psalms 34:10).

**The second** — the master of alchemy is in need of works and crafts without which his sought-after end is not made valid for him. Their fumes and vapors may kill him, along with the perpetuity of the labor and the continuity of fatigue in them, night and day. The one who relies on God is in safety from misfortunes, in ease of mind from the descending of calamities; and whatever comes upon him from God (exalted be He) is a delight and joy to him; his sustenance comes to him with pleasantness of life, repose, and tranquility, as He said: "He makes me lie down in pastures of green grass; He leads me beside still waters" (Psalms 23:2).

**The third** — the master of alchemy cannot trust his secret with another, out of fear for himself. The one who relies on God fears no one for his reliance; rather he glories in it, as the Friend said: "In God I have trusted; I will not fear what the human being can do to me" (Psalms 56:12).

**The fourth** — the master of alchemy must either store up much silver and gold for the time of his need, or store up of them only the measure that suffices him for a brief while. If he stores up much of it, he is throughout his lifetime in a state of fear of its loss to him through the various causes of loss; his mind is not settled, nor his soul at ease, out of fear for it from the king and from the populace. If he stores up only what would close the gap of his lack for a brief while, perhaps the work will become impossible for him just when he is in greatest need of it, on account of some impediment among its causes coming upon him. The one who relies on God has strength of confidence in God: that He sustains him with what He wills, when He wills, and from where He wills — as He sustains the embryo in the womb, and the chick in the belly of the egg, which has no opening to it from outside, and the bird in the air, and the fish in the water, and the ant and the worm in their weakness; while sustenance becomes impossible for the lion in his strength on certain days — as David said: "The young lions go without and starve" (Psalms 34:11); and: "The Lord shall not let the soul of the righteous starve" (Proverbs 10:3); and: "I have been young and I have grown old; and I have not seen the righteous abandoned, nor his seed seeking bread" (Psalms 37:25).

**The fifth** — the master of alchemy is under fear and watch over his craft from the king and down to the lowest of his subjects. The one who relies on God — kings and the great among people fear him; even the non-rational animal, and even the inanimate seeks his approval — as the Friend said: "He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High, who lodges in the shadow of the Almighty…" to the end of the psalm (Psalms 91); and He said: "In six troubles He shall deliver you, and in seven evil shall not touch you: in famine He shall redeem you from death" — to the end of the chapter (Job 5:19–22).

**The sixth** — the master of alchemy is not safe from sicknesses and ailments that spoil his joy by their assault, so that he profits not from what he has and takes no pleasure in what his two hands have garnered. The one who relies on God is in safety from ailments and sicknesses — except by way of refining or recompense — as He said: "Youths shall faint and grow weary, and chosen men shall surely stumble, but those who hope in the Lord shall renew strength" (Isaiah 40:30–31); and He said: "For the arms of the wicked shall be broken, but the Lord upholds the righteous" (Psalms 37:17).

**The seventh** — the master of alchemy may be unable to reach his nourishment with the gold and silver he has, on account of the absence of food in his land at certain times, as He said: "They shall throw their silver into the streets, and their gold shall become an unclean thing… their silver and their gold shall not be able to deliver them" (Ezekiel 7:19). The one who relies on God — his nourishment is never impossible for him at any time and in any place, until the conclusion of his term, as He said: "In famine He shall redeem you from death, and in war from the hands of the sword" (Job 5:20); and He said: "The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not lack" (Psalms 23:1); and He said: "They shall not be put to shame in the time of evil, and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied" (Psalms 37:19).

**The eighth** — the master of alchemy cannot settle in any place out of fear of his secret being uncovered. The one who relies on God is at peace in his land, settled of soul in his place, as He said: "Trust in the Lord and do good; dwell in the land and pasture in faithfulness" (Psalms 37:3); and He said: "The righteous shall inherit the land and dwell upon it forever" (Psalms 37:29).

**The ninth** — the master of alchemy is not accompanied in the next world by his alchemy; he attains from it in this world only his nourishment and the safety from poverty and from need of people. The one who relies on God is accompanied by the reward of his reliance in this world and the next, as He said: "And he who trusts in the Lord — kindness shall surround him" (Psalms 32:10); and He said: "How abundant is Your goodness, which You have stored up for those who fear You" (Psalms 31:20).

**The tenth** — the master of alchemy, if he makes his affair public, this becomes the cause of his perishing and his destruction; for in what flows toward him and is gathered upon him there is a contradiction of the order of the world. The Orderer of the All sets one against him who will kill him if he does not skillfully conceal his secret. The one who relies on God, if he makes his reliance public, is exalted in the eyes of the creatures; people honor him, and they are blessed by his nearness and the sight of him; he becomes a cause of the welfare of his land and the warding off of misfortunes from the people of his place, as He said: "And the righteous is the foundation of the world" (Proverbs 10:25), as in the story of Lot at Zoar (Genesis 19:20–22).

Among the benefits of reliance on God (mighty and exalted) in religion, also: that the one who relies on God (exalted be He) — if he is a possessor of wealth — hastens to bring forth the dues of God and the dues of people from his wealth, with openhandedness of soul and graciousness of disposition. And if he has no wealth, he sees the absence of wealth as a blessing from God upon him, on account of the falling away from him of the obligations binding upon him in it toward God and toward people, and on account of the slightness of his preoccupation in keeping and managing it. As it was said of one of the righteous, that he used to say: "I take refuge in God from the dispersion of the soul." It was said to him: "And what is the dispersion of the soul?" He said: "That I should have wealth at the head of every valley and in every village." And it is the saying of our early ones: "Whoever multiplies possessions multiplies anxiety" (m. Avot 2:7), and they said: "Who is rich? He who is content with his portion" (m. Avot 4:1). The one who relies on God attains the gains of wealth — namely, his sustenance — and is spared the preoccupation of mind of the possessor of wealth and the long burden of his concern for it, as the Wise One said: "Sweet is the sleep of the laborer, whether he eats little or much; but the satiety of the rich does not let him sleep" (Ecclesiastes 5:11).

Among them: that the abundance of wealth does not prevent the one who relies on God from relying on God, since he does not lean upon his wealth — and it is, in his sight, in the form of a deposit which he has been commanded to disburse in specific ways and on specific affairs, for a fixed term. If its remaining with him endures, it does not make him insolent, nor does he reproach with it the one to whom he has been commanded to deliver some of it, nor seek thanks and praise for that — but rather he thanks God who has made him a means for benefits. If the wealth perishes from him, he does not grieve over it nor become sad at its loss, but thanks God for the recovery of His deposit just as he praised Him at His handing it over to him; he is content with his condition, neither overstepping toward another nor envying anyone in his wealth, as the Wise One said: "The righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" (Proverbs 13:25).

As for the benefits of reliance on God in this world: among them is the repose of the heart from worldly anxieties, and the rest from the agitation and disquiet of the soul over the loss of its bodily beloveds. He is in a state of tranquility and quiet, in safety from the world, as He said: "Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and whose trust is the Lord; he shall be like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by a stream" (Jeremiah 17:7–8). Among them is the rest of his body from long journeys that wear out bodies and hasten the end of lives, as Scripture said of him: "He has weakened my strength on the way, He has shortened my days" (Psalms 102:24). And it has been related of one of the people of asceticism that, at the start of his affair, he traveled to a far land in pursuit of sustenance. He met a man of those who worship idols in the land to which he had traveled. The ascetic said to him: "You are at the extreme of blindness and lack of discrimination in your worship of these images." The Magian said to him: "And what is it that you worship?" The ascetic said: "I worship the Creator, the Powerful, the Sufficient, the One, the Provider, beside whom there is nothing like Him." The Magian said to him: "Your action contradicts your speech." The ascetic said: "How is that?" The Magian said: "If what you have claimed were certainty, He would have provided you in your land as He provides you here, and you would not have wearied yourself by coming to this land over the long distance between them." The ascetic was cut off from his proof; he turned back to his land, bound himself to asceticism from that hour, and did not travel after that.

Among them: the rest of soul and body from grueling labors and crafts that exhaust bodies, and the abandonment of binding-oneself to the service of kings in their formal duties and the oppression of their subjects. The one who relies on God exposes himself only to those of the causes of sustenance most restful for his body, most ample for his standing, most easeful to his mind, and most fitting for the upholding of the requirements of his Law — together with the soundness of his certainty that the cause neither adds anything to his sustenance nor diminishes from it, except by the decree of God (exalted be He), as He said: "For not from the east and not from the west, and not from the wilderness of mountains; but God is the judge: this one He brings down and that one He raises up" (Psalms 75:7–8); and He said: "He makes me lie down in pastures of green grass; He leads me beside still waters" (Psalms 23:2).

Among them: the slightness of disquiet of his soul over his commerce, the standstill of his merchandise, the impossibility of collecting a debt, or sickness when it falls upon his body — for his knowledge that God is wiser concerning his affairs than he is, and better in choice for him than he is for himself, as He said: "But for God my soul waits in silence; for from Him is my hope" (Psalms 62:6). Among them: joy in every state into which he is moved, even if his nature is repelled by it — out of confidence in God that He does not act with him except in what is most fitting of matters for him, as the merciful mother acts with her child in his washing, his cleaning, his swaddling and his binding, despite his loathing of it, as the Friend (peace be upon him) said: "If I have not stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child upon its mother — like a weaned child upon me is my soul" (Psalms 131:2).
Now that I have explicated, of the benefits of reliance on God and its profits in religion and worldly life, what has come to mind, let us set forth from the matter of reliance seven things:

1. **The first**: the quiddity of reliance. 2. **The second**: on the causes of reliance upon created beings. 3. **The third**: on the explication of the premises that necessitate reliance on God, and the obligation of engagement with the means. 4. **The fourth**: on the explication of the matters in which reliance takes place, and the obligation of its goodness and badness in them. 5. **The fifth**: on the section concerning the difference between the engagement of the one who relies on God with the means of sustenance, and the engagement of the one who does not rely on God with them. 6. **The sixth**: on the explication of the aspects of the obligatory ugliness of the school of those who say there is length to hope in this world, and who promise themselves the binding-on of obedience to God when they have reached their hope in it — these are the people of pawned-pledges. 7. **The seventh**: on the corrupters of reliance on God, and the summary statement of the meaning of reliance and a brief abridgment of its divisions.
As for the quiddity of reliance —

It is the repose of the soul of the one who relies, and the leaning of his heart upon the One relied upon, that He will do with him what is most fitting and most agreeable for him in the matter in which he relies upon Him, according to His capacity and His knowledge of what agrees with him.

As for the principle from which reliance arises in the one who relies — and which, when absent, the reliance is no longer existent — it is confidence in the One relied upon: that He fulfills what He has said, and does what He has guaranteed; together with good opinion of Him in what He has not stipulated nor guaranteed He would do, that He is doing it as a favor and a kindness.
As for the causes by which reliance is made valid in the one who relies upon created beings — they are seven.

**The first** — mercy, compassion, sympathy, and love. For the human being, when he knows of another that he is merciful and compassionate toward him, has confidence in him, and his soul reposes upon him in what he commits to him of his affairs.

**The second** — that, along with his love for him, he has known him not to be heedless of him nor to neglect his need; rather, he has come to know him as resolute and determined in this. For if this is not made valid for him concerning the trustee, his reliance upon him is not complete, since he knows of his heedlessness and slackness in his needs. When these two qualities are gathered for the one relying in the one upon whom he relies — namely, the intensity of mercy upon him and the strength of attentiveness to his affairs — he relies on him without fail.

**The third** — that the one upon whom one relies be strong, not overcome in his will, nor prevented by anything from carrying out his need. For if he is weak, reliance upon him is not complete, even if compassion and attentiveness are sound from him, on account of the impossibility of matters for him in most cases. When these three qualities are gathered in him, reliance upon him becomes more obligatory.

**The fourth** — that the one upon whom one relies be knowledgeable of the aspects of the welfare of the one relying upon him, not ignorant of what agrees with him in his inner and outer state and what would set his condition right. For when he is ignorant of this, the soul of the one relying does not repose upon him in this respect. When the knowledge of his welfare and the power over it and the intensity of attentiveness to him and compassion upon him are gathered in him, his reliance upon him grows strong without fail.

**The fifth** — that the one upon whom one relies has uniquely managed the affair of the one relying from the beginning of his being and his coming-to-be — his infancy, his childhood, his youth, his maturity, and his old age — to the conclusion of his affair. When this has been made valid for the one relying, his soul's repose upon him and his leaning upon him are obligatory, on account of the antecedent blessings and the successive benefits he has received from him; and this is among what makes the emphasis of reliance upon him obligatory.

**The sixth** — that the affair of the one relying be wholly committed to the one upon whom he relies, no one else being able to harm him or to benefit him, nor capable of beneficence to him or of warding off the disliked from him — like the imprisoned slave under the authority of his master. When the one relying is in the disposition of the one upon whom he relies in this state, he is more emphatic and more rightful for reliance upon him.

**The seventh** — that the one upon whom one relies be at the utmost of generosity and at the limit of bounty toward the one who deserves it and the one who does not deserve it; and that his generosity be successive and his bounty continuous, neither cut off nor severed.

In whom all of this has been gathered, together with what has been mentioned before, the conditions of reliance in him have been completed. And it is incumbent upon the one who has known this of him to rely upon him and to repose upon him in his outer and inner state, in his heart and his limbs; to surrender to him; to be content with his decree; and to have good opinion of him in all his judgments and his actions.

When we examine these seven conditions, we do not find them gathered in created beings. We find them all in the Creator (exalted be He). As for His being merciful to His creatures: as He said, "Merciful and gracious is the Lord" (Psalms 103:8); and He said, "And shall I not have pity on Nineveh, the great city?" (Jonah 4:11). As for His being not heedless: as the Friend (peace be upon him) said, "Behold, He neither slumbers nor sleeps, the Keeper of Israel" (Psalms 121:4). As for His being not ignorant and not overcome: as He said, "Wise of heart and mighty in strength — who has hardened himself against Him and remained whole?" (Job 9:4); and He said, "Yours, O Lord, is the greatness, and the power, and the splendor, and the victory, and the majesty" (1 Chronicles 29:11); and He said, "The Lord your God is in your midst, a mighty One who saves" (Zephaniah 3:17). As for His being unique in the management of the human from the beginning of his affair and the start of his being: as Scripture said, "Is He not your father who has acquired you? He has made you and established you" (Deuteronomy 32:6); and He said, "Upon You I was sustained from the womb; from my mother's belly You are my support" (Psalms 71:6); and He said, "Did You not pour me out as milk and curdle me like cheese?" (Job 10:10), and the rest of the passage. As for His benefit and harm being subject to no one's authority but the Creator's (exalted be He): as Scripture said, "Who can speak and have it come to be, if the Lord has not commanded? From the mouth of the Most High does not the bad and the good go forth?" (Lamentations 3:37–38); and He said, "The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God shall stand forever" (Isaiah 40:8); and He said, "Surely the people are grass" (Isaiah 40:7) — and this concept has been validly established in the Third Treatise of this book sufficiently. As for His generosity being general and His bounty extending to all: as He said, "Good is the Lord to all, and His mercy is upon all His works" (Psalms 145:9); and He said, "Who gives bread to all flesh, for His mercy endures forever" (Psalms 136:25); and He said, "You open Your hand and satisfy every living thing with favor" (Psalms 145:16). The intellect itself decides that these seven concepts are gathered in the Creator (exalted be He) to the exclusion of created beings; but I have brought in these *pesuqim* from the Book by way of recollection only.

When this has become validly established for the human, and his discrimination of the true reality of the Creator (exalted be He) has grown strong, he relies upon Him, surrenders to Him, casts upon Him the management of his affair, does not impugn Him in His wisdom, and is not dissatisfied at His choice for him — as the Friend said, "I shall lift up the cup of salvation, and I shall call upon the name of the Lord" (Psalms 116:13); and he said, "I have found distress and sorrow, and I shall call upon the name of the Lord" (Psalms 116:3–4).
As for the premises by the soundness and certainty of which reliance upon God (exalted be He) is completed for the human — they are five.

**The first** — his firm conviction and verification of the gathering of the seven concepts in God (mighty and exalted), by whose gathering in the trustee reliance upon him is made valid for the one relying. I have already mentioned them and called attention to them by what came to my mind from the Truthful Book.

These are: that God (exalted be He) is the most merciful of the merciful upon the human, and that every mercy and compassion that comes to him from another is from the mercy of God (exalted be He) and His tenderness, as Scripture said, "And He shall give you mercies, and have mercy upon you, and multiply you" (Deuteronomy 13:18). The second: that the Creator (exalted be He) is not ignorant of the aspects of the welfare of the human; necessarily so, since the human is among His made things, and none can be more knowledgeable of the aspects of welfare and corruption of the made thing — and of the misfortunes that befall it, and of the aspects of its remedy and its cure — than its Maker. If this is found among the craftsmen of people, who originate in their made things only an accidental form (for as for the matter and the substantial form they have no contrivance or power of derivation in them), then He who created the matters of the human, his form, his constitution, and the order of his composition is more knowledgeable and wiser of the kinds of his benefits and harms and of what agrees with him in his this-world and his next-world, without fail — as He said, "I am the Lord your God, who teaches you to profit, who leads you in the way you should go" (Isaiah 48:17); and He said, "For whom the Lord loves He reproves" (Proverbs 3:12). The third: that the Creator (exalted be He) is the strongest of every strong, and His command is more piercing than every command, and there is no rejecting His wisdom — as He said, "All that the Lord wills, He has done" (Psalms 135:6); and He said, "So shall My word be that goes forth from My mouth — it shall not return to Me empty, but shall do that which I willed" (Isaiah 55:11). The fourth: that He is solicitous of the management of the affairs of the human, every one of them — neither neglects them nor is heedless of them, nor is anything of their fine details or their grand outlines hidden from Him, nor does anything cause Him to forget anything — as He said, "Why do you say, O Jacob, and why do you speak, O Israel: 'My way is hidden from the Lord, and my justice is overlooked by my God'? Have you not known? have you not heard? The eternal God, the Lord, the Creator of the ends of the earth, neither faints nor grows weary; there is no searching out His understanding" (Isaiah 40:27–28). The fifth: that nothing is in the hand of any of created beings — neither benefit to themselves nor harm to themselves, nor to others — except by the permission of God (exalted be He). For when a slave has more than one master, and each one of them is capable of his benefit and harm, his reliance upon any one of them is not made valid, since he hopes for benefit from each of them. If one of them is more capable of this than the rest, the strength of his reliance upon him will be in proportion to that — even if his reliance upon the rest [also obtains]. When none but one of them alone is capable of his benefit and harm, by necessity he relies on him alone, since he hopes for no benefit from another. So too, when the human realizes that none of created beings benefits him or harms him except by the permission of God (exalted be He), his heart turns away from fear of them and hope in them, and he relies on the Creator (mighty and exalted) alone, as He said, "Trust not in nobles, in the son of man, who has no salvation" (Psalms 146:3). The sixth: that he know the magnitude of His blessing upon the human, and that with which He has begun him of abundant bounty and beneficence — without prior deserving from him before Him, and without need from Him for him; but rather as generosity and beneficence, bounty and graciousness, as we have laid out in the Gate of Reflection of this book — as the Friend (peace be upon him) said, "You have done many things, O Lord my God: Your wonders and Your thoughts toward us — there is none to compare to You; were I to declare and speak them, they are too many to be told" (Psalms 40:6).

The seventh — that it be made valid for him that for everything intended in this world — substance or accident — there is a known limit, neither exceeding nor falling short of what the Creator (exalted be He) has decreed in its quantity, its quality, its time, and its place: no one multiplies what He has decreed to be made few, nor diminishes what He has decreed to be made many; no one delays what He has decreed to advance, nor advances what He has decreed to delay. Whatever among the matters is otherwise — that is the decreed thing that has gone before in foreknowledge. Yet for all the prior decrees in the knowledge of God (mighty and exalted), there are causes; and the causes have causes. He who is ignorant of the affairs of the world supposes that the proximate cause necessitates the change of matters and their reversal from one state to another, while the cause is too weak and slight for change or transformation in itself to come from it.

For instance, we see one grain of wheat, from which sprout three hundred ears, in each ear about thirty grains — so that one grain becomes the cause of ten thousand grains and thereabouts. Is the weakness of the grain hidden, given the like of this? And so for the rest of the seeded and planted grains. Likewise the speech concerning the coming-to-be of the body of the human and the rest of the animal from a drop of seed; and like it, the bringing-into-being of a great fish from the egg of a fish, in its weakness. The preoccupation of the soul with advancing what God has delayed, and delaying what He has advanced, and multiplying what He has made little, and diminishing what He has multiplied, of the goods of this world — apart from causing-oneself to fulfill the obligations of His obedience and to bind oneself to His Law — is a weakness of discrimination concerning the true reality of His knowledge, and an ignorance of the goodness of His care for us. The Wise One has gestured at this concept with his saying: "For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under the heavens" (Ecclesiastes 3:1). Then he mentioned twenty-eight concepts under it, namely his saying: "A time to be born and a time to die" up to "a time of war and a time of peace" (Ecclesiastes 3:2–8); and he said: "For time and chance happen to them all" (Ecclesiastes 9:11); and he said: "For high one is above high one watches, and there are higher ones above them" (Ecclesiastes 5:7). The currents of the judgments of the Creator (exalted be He) are more hidden, more concealed, and more exalted than that we should reach knowledge of their particulars — let alone their universals; and Scripture has said: "For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are My ways higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts" (Isaiah 55:9).

**The second premise** — his knowledge and verification that God (mighty and exalted) is overseeing him, and nothing is hidden from Him of his outer and inner, his secret and his manifest, of his purification in his reliance upon his Lord or the absence of his purification in it — as Scripture said, "The Lord knows the thoughts of man, that they are vapor" (Psalms 94:11); and He said, "Behold, He weighs hearts; does He not understand?" (Proverbs 24:12); and He said, "For You alone know the heart of all the children of man" (1 Kings 8:39). When the one relying has verified this, it does not become valid for him to claim reliance on God (exalted be He) by his speech without his relying on Him with his heart and his inner being; for he would then be of the rank of the one of whom it was said: "With his mouth and his lips they have honored Me, but their heart is far from Me" (Isaiah 29:13).

**The third premise** — singling out his Lord by reliance upon Him in what reliance is incumbent upon him in, and not associating another with Him in it — so that he relies upon Him together with one of created beings, by which his reliance upon God would be corrupted, since he has associated another with Him. You have learned what Scripture said about Asa, despite his bounty, when he leaned upon physicians, in his saying: "And in his sickness he did not seek the Lord, but the physicians" (2 Chronicles 16:12), and he was punished for this. And Scripture said: "Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and whose trust is the Lord" (Jeremiah 17:7). It is known that anyone among people who has appointed two trustees for the carrying-out of one of his affairs — or more than that — his reliance is corrupted; how much more so the one who has relied on God and on something other than Him: he has corrupted his reliance, and that becomes the strongest cause of his being denied the carrying-out of what he relied upon Him for, as Scripture said: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm" (Jeremiah 17:5).

**The fourth premise** — that he be intense in attentiveness and exertion in the upholding of what God (exalted be He, mighty and exalted) has bound him to of His obedience and the working at His commandments, and the desisting from what He has prohibited — according to what he wishes God to be for him in what he has relied upon Him for, as our early ones (peace be upon them) said: "Make His will as your will, that He may make your will as His will; nullify your will before His will, that He may nullify the will of others before your will" (m. Avot 2:4); and Scripture said, "Trust in the Lord and do good; dwell in the land and pasture in faithfulness" (Psalms 37:3); and He said, "Good is the Lord to those who hope in Him, to the soul that seeks Him" (Lamentations 3:25). As for the one who relies on God while he disobeys Him — how ignorant he is, how slight his intellect and his discrimination! For he sees that one who has had something committed to him by people, when he is bound to the carrying out of one of his needs, or prohibited from a certain matter — and he transgresses what was set as a limit for him, and this is conveyed to the trustee — his violation of his command is the strongest cause of his being denied the carrying-out of what he had relied upon him for. How much more, then — and more emphatic — is the transgression of the limits and obligations of God, in those things over which He has promised reward and warned of punishment, that the hope of the one relying upon Him be disappointed when he disobeys Him: he does not deserve the name of "one who relies on God"; rather he is as Scripture said: "For what is the hope of the impious, when he gains, when God draws out his soul? Will God hear his cry?" (Job 27:8–9); and He said: "Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, burn incense to Baal, and follow other gods whom you have not known — and then come and stand before Me in this house upon which My name is called, and say 'we are delivered' — that you may do all these abominations? Has this house become a den of robbers?" (Jeremiah 7:9–11).

**The fifth premise** — that it be made valid for him that the completion of the events that come to be in this world after creation is by two matters. The one of them, the decree of the Creator (exalted be He) and His will for their going forth into the bounds of being from non-being. The second, causes and intermediaries — among them proximate, among them remote; among them manifest, among them hidden — all of them flowing toward the completion of what He has decreed to come to be and appear, by God's aid given to them for that.

The image of proximate causes, in the drawing forth of water from the depth of the earth by the wheel, is in the buckets that lift the water by the well-mechanism from the well. As for its remote cause, it is the human who yokes the beast to the well-mechanism, who moves it to lift the water from the bottom of the well to the surface of the earth. As for the causes between the human and the buckets, they are intermediaries between the two matters: the beast, the gears that turn one another, and the rope. If a defect befalls one of the mentioned causes, the intended purpose is not completed by them. So too the rest of the actions flowing into the bound of being: they are made valid by the human and another only by the decree of God (exalted be He) and His enabling them with the causes by which their completion comes — as He said: "For a God of knowledge is the Lord, and by Him deeds are weighed" (1 Samuel 2:3); and He said: "Great in counsel and abundant in deed" (Jeremiah 32:19); and He said: "For it was a turn of events from the Lord" (1 Kings 12:15). When the causes are wholly absent, the going-forth of the thing from the natural actions to the bound of being is not completed.

When we have considered the necessity of the human to the engagement and the causing for the completion of his matters, we find it going forth into plain sight: for the one who needs nourishment, when food has been set in front of him in what agrees with him — if he does not engage with eating it by lifting it to his mouth and chewing it — the gap of his hunger is not closed; and so the thirsty one in his need of water. How much, then, when food becomes impossible to him without his engaging with its preparation by grinding, kneading, cooking, and the like; and stronger and more emphatic is the engagement, if he needs to purchase it and prepare it; and yet more, if the price by which he buys it is impossible to him: he needs an engagement and a causing stronger than what was mentioned before — either he hires himself out for the price, or he sells what he cannot do without of furniture and goods and the like.

The reason on account of which God has bound the human to engagement with the causes of sustenance and of the rest of what he needs is twofold. The first: because wisdom required the testing of the soul in this world by obedience and disobedience; He has tried it with what makes that manifest from it — namely, neediness and want for what is outside it of food and drink and clothing and dwelling and marriage. He has commanded it to engage in attracting these by the causes prepared for it in specific aspects and at known times. What God has decreed to be completed for the human of these is completed and made valid by the soundness of the coming of the causes; what God has not decreed to be completed for him is not completed, and the causes become impossible for him; and obedience and disobedience to God (mighty and exalted) are validly attributed to him by intent and choice for one of them and not the other, and that necessitates reward and punishment, even if the carrying-out of the act has not been validly completed by the human.

The second aspect: that if the human were spared the toil and engagement and causing in attracting his sustenance, he would exult and grow insolent, and hasten to acts of disobedience, and pay no regard to the dues of the blessings of God upon him — as He said: "And there shall be lyre and lute, drum and pipe, and wine at their banquets — but the work of the Lord they regard not, and the deed of His hands they do not see" (Isaiah 5:12); and He said: "And Jeshurun grew fat and kicked; you grew fat, gross, gorged, and he forsook the God who made him" (Deuteronomy 32:15). The early ones said: "Beautiful is the study of the Law together with worldly occupation, for the labor of both makes sin be forgotten; and any Torah without occupation alongside it — its end is annulment, and it draws sin in its wake" (m. Avot 2:2); and more rightful is the one deprived of both, his mind preoccupied with neither.

So it was of the gentleness of the Creator (exalted be He) toward the human that He preoccupied him with the affairs of his this-world and his next-world, that he might be occupied throughout the span of his life with that — and not seek what does not concern him and what his intellect cannot grasp, such as the matters of beginning and end, as He said: "He has even put the world into their heart, without which the human cannot find out the work that God has done from beginning to end" (Ecclesiastes 3:11). If, then, he is one who prefers obedience to God, who chooses His worship, who relies upon Him in the affairs of his religion and his worldly life — withdrawing from vile traits, longing for excellences, neither exulting in ease nor at home in slackness, neither seized by appetite nor deceived by the world's enchantment — the burden of engagement and causing for the attraction of his sustenance falls away from him, on account of the falling away from him of the two aspects mentioned, namely, the testing and the insolent boasting in the blessing. His sustenance comes to him without weariness or burden, in proportion to need and subsistence, as He said: "The Lord shall not let the soul of the righteous starve" (Proverbs 10:3).

If a speaker should say: "We see some of the righteous whose sustenance is not made ready for them except after burden and weariness; and many of the people of disobedience are at ease, and their living is the most prosperous and pleasant" — I say: this concept has already been investigated by the prophets and the excellent ones. Among them is one who said: "Why does the way of the wicked prosper?" (Jeremiah 12:1); and another said: "Why do You make me see iniquity, and look upon trouble — destruction and violence are before me; there is contention, and strife arises" (Habakkuk 1:3); and he said: "When the wicked surrounds the righteous" (Habakkuk 1:4); and: "Why do You keep silent when the wicked swallows the righteous more righteous than he?" (Habakkuk 1:13). Another said: "Behold, these are the wicked, and ever at ease they have grown rich" (Psalms 73:12); and: "Surely in vain have I purified my heart and washed my hands in innocence; for I have been afflicted all the day, and my chastisement comes in the mornings" (Psalms 73:13–14). Another said, on the tongue of the people of his time: "They have built up the doers of wickedness; they have even tested God and escaped" (Malachi 3:15) — and many like that.

But the Prophet abbreviated the answer concerning the explication of the cause of this, since the cause of each one of the righteous tested, and of each one of the wicked enjoying blessing in this world, is other than the cause of the others. Yet he gestured at this with his saying: "The hidden things belong to the Lord our God, but the revealed things belong to us and to our children" (Deuteronomy 29:28). The Wise One said, in the like of this: "If you see the oppression of the poor and the violent perversion of justice and right in a province, do not be amazed at the matter" (Ecclesiastes 5:7); and Scripture said: "The Rock — His work is perfect, for all His ways are justice" (Deuteronomy 32:4).

Even so, I see that I should make plain in this what is in some measure persuasive. I say: the aspect on account of which the sustenance of the excellent one becomes impossible — to the point that he is afflicted in it and tested by it — may be on account of a sin that preceded him, for which it was incumbent that he be requited for it, as He said: "Behold, the righteous one shall be requited in the earth — how much more the wicked and the sinner!" (Proverbs 11:31). And it may be by way of recompense in the next world, as He said: "That He might afflict you, that He might test you, to do you good in your latter end" (Deuteronomy 8:16). And it may be that his patience and the goodness of his bearing in obedience to God become manifest, that people may pattern themselves after him, as you have learned from the story of Job. And it may be on account of the disobedience of the people of his time toward God: God tries him with poverty and need and sickness, that his excellence and his obedience to God in distinction from them may be made manifest, as He said: "Surely our sicknesses he has borne, and our pains he has carried; yet we accounted him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted" (Isaiah 53:4). And it may be on account of the slightness of his championing the dues of God from the people of his time, as you have learned from the story of Eli and his sons, of whom Scripture said: "And every one that is left in your house shall come and bow down to him for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread" (1 Samuel 2:36).

As for the blessing of God upon the disobedient: it may be for some good that preceded him — God recompensing him for it in this world — as He said: "And He repays those who hate Him to their face, to destroy them" (Deuteronomy 7:10), and our early ones translated it: "*And He repays those who hate Him — the merits they have done before Him in their lifetimes — to destroy them; He does not delay the good deed of those who hate Him; the merits they have done before Him in their lifetime, He repays to them*." And it may be by way of a deposit with him, until God provides him with a righteous son who deserves it, as He said: "He prepares it, and the righteous puts it on" (Job 27:17), and: "And to the sinner He gives the business of gathering and amassing — to give to the one who is good before God" (Ecclesiastes 2:26). And it may be for the greatest cause of his perishing and his trial, as He said: "Wealth kept by its owner to his harm" (Ecclesiastes 5:12). And it may be God's granting him reprieve that he might repent and become deserving of it, as you have learned from the story of Manasseh. And it may be for an excellence that preceded in his ancestor, so that he deserved that he be blessed for the sake of his son — as He said to Jehu son of Nimshi: "Sons of the fourth generation shall sit for you on the throne of Israel" (2 Kings 10:30); and He said: "He who walks in his integrity is righteous; happy are his children after him" (Proverbs 20:7); and: "I have been young and I have grown old; and I have not seen the righteous abandoned, nor his seed seeking bread" (Psalms 37:25). And it may be for the testing of the people of evil interiors and corrupt inward states: when they see this, they hasten to the contrary of obedience and rush to flatter them and pattern themselves after their actions; and the pure for God become refined, and the truthful in his obedience to God in his patience under their overbearing and their reproach is made manifest. The recompense for that comes down from God (exalted be He), as you have learned from the story of Elijah with Jezebel, and Jeremiah with the heads of the people of his time.

Now, since the obligation of engagement with the causes upon people has become valid, let us make plain that not every human is bound to engage with every cause among the causes of sustenance. The causes are very many. Among them are easy ones, slight in burden — like trade in a shop, or a craft of the hand light in burden, like sewing and patching and writing, and like the merchant by his hoarding-and-trading of goods, and the wages of partners and hands and those engaged in the cultivation of the earth. Among them are causes in which there is burden and toil, like the craft of tanning the hide, and the extracting of iron and copper and lead from their mines, and the refining of silver with lead, and the carrying of heavy loads, and the succession of journeys, and the service of the earth and its tilling, and the like.

Whoever among people is strong in body and weak in discrimination, that of them which fits him, in proportion to his bearing, is the labor of the works of toil. And whoever is weak of body and strong of discrimination — let him not engage with the causes of sustenance with what wearies his body, but rather incline from them to what is light upon his body and to what permits him perpetuity in it. And every human has an eagerness for some craft or some commerce, to the exclusion of others, which God has stamped-by-nature in his constitution as a love and a preference. So too in the rest of the animal: as He has stamped in the constitution of the cat the hunting of mice, and in the constitution of the falcon the hunting of birds resembling it, and in the constitution of the deer the hunting of snakes; and so among the birds, some hunt fish only; and so in the constitution of every species among the species of the animal there is an inclination and an appetite for a species among the species of plants and animals which it has been stamped-by-nature for, that it may be a cause for its nourishment. He has prepared its body and its instruments to match that — like the long beak and the long leg for the bird that hunts the fish; like the fang and the strong claws for the lion; like the horns for the bull and the deer. The one whose nourishment depends upon plants — the instruments of hunting and the implements of seizing-and-tearing have been withheld from him.

On this same model, you find the dispositions of people and their bodies prepared for trades and crafts. So whoever finds in his constitution and his nature a longing for a craft among the crafts, his body agreeing with it in bearing the burden of its labor — let him engage with it and make it the cause of attracting his subsistence; let him bear with patience its sweetness and its bitterness; let him not become anxious if sustenance becomes impossible for him at some times, but let him rely on God (exalted be He) to bestow upon him his sustenance throughout his span. Let him aim, in the preoccupation of his mind and his body with one of the causes and engagement with them, at submission to the command of God who has commanded the human to use the causes in the world — like the cultivation of the earth, its service, and its sowing, as He said: "And the Lord God took the human and set him in the garden of Eden to work it and to keep it" (Genesis 2:15); and the use of animals in his welfares and his nourishment; and the building of cities and the preparation of provisions; and the use of women and marrying them, that progeny might multiply. He will be rewarded for his aim therein at the face of God, with his heart and his intent — whether what he has sought is completed for him, or it becomes impossible — as the Friend (peace be upon him) said: "When you eat the labor of your hands, happy are you, and it is well with you" (Psalms 128:2); and the early ones (peace be upon them) said: "And let all your works be for the sake of Heaven" (m. Avot 2:12).

His reliance upon God is thereby made valid; the engagement with the causes for the attraction of his sustenance by means of them does not harm him at all, when he aims with his inner being and his intent at the face of God in them. He should not suppose that his sustenance is bound to a particular cause — and that whenever this becomes impossible for him, it cannot come to be by another cause — but rather let him rely on God in his sustenance, and know that the causes are, with God, all alike: He sustains him with what He wills, from where He wills, as Scripture said: "For there is no constraint with the Lord to save by many or by few" (1 Samuel 14:6); and He said: "For He is the One who gives you power to act with might" (Deuteronomy 8:18); and He said: "Not by valor and not by power, but by My spirit, says the Lord of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6).

As for the matters in which it is incumbent upon the believer to rely upon God: all of them are of two kinds. The one of them, the matters of this world; the second, the matters of the next world. The matters of this world are divided into two divisions: the one of them, matters of this world for the welfare of this world; the second, matters of this world for the welfare of the next world.

The matters of this world for the welfare of this world are divided into three divisions: the one, the welfares of his bodily affairs alone; the second division, the welfares of his sustenance and the causes of his earning and the kinds of his properties; the third division, the welfares of his household, his dependents, his relations, his brothers, his enemies, and those above him and below him among the ranks of people.

As for the matters of this world for the welfare of the next world, they are divided into two divisions: the one of them, the duties of the heart and the limbs that pertain to him alone — his action in them does not extend, in benefit or harm, to another. The second division, the duties of the limbs that are made valid only by another's participation with him in act and patient-receiving — like charity, doing-the-beautiful, the spreading of knowledge, commanding the right, and forbidding the wrong.

As for the matters of the next world, they are divided into two divisions: the one of them, the deserved reward; the second, the reward bestowed as a favor upon the saints and the prophets in the next world. So the matters in which one relies on God are, in sum, seven divisions:

1. **The first** — the affairs of the body of the human in particular. 2. **The second** — the affairs of his earning and the causes of his sustenance. 3. **The third** — the affairs of his dependents, his children, his relations, his friends, and his enemies. 4. **The fourth** — the duties of the heart and the limbs whose benefit and harm are restricted to him. 5. **The fifth** — the duties of the limbs whose benefit and harm pass beyond him to another. 6. **The sixth** — the reward of the next world that is according to deed in this world. 7. **The seventh** — the reward of the next world that is from God by way of bounty upon His elect and His saints, as He said: "How abundant is Your goodness, which You have stored up for those who fear You; You have done for those who hope in You before the children of men" (Psalms 31:20).

Since I have explicated for you the premises by which reliance is made valid for the one who relies on God (mighty and exalted), it is now incumbent that I follow that with the explication of the aspects of right reliance in each one of the seven matters in which every one who relies on God or another relies, one after another.

I say, in the explication of the first division — namely, the affairs of the body of the human in particular: that is his life, his death, and the sustenance of his nourishment for his subsistence; his clothing, his dwelling, his health, his sickness, and his traits.

The aspect of right reliance on God (mighty and exalted) in everything of this is that he cast himself in them upon the currents of the decree that God has decreed for him in them; that his soul repose upon God (mighty and exalted), that nothing is completed for him from these matters except what has gone before in the knowledge of God (exalted be He) as most agreeable to his condition in this world and the next, and most fitting for his outcome; that the management of all of them is from God for him alone — no created being has any management or measuring in them except by the permission of God (exalted be He), by His power and His wisdom. For just as his life, his death, his sickness, and his health are not in the hand of created beings, so too the sustenance of his nourishment, his subsistence, his clothing, and the rest of the affairs of his body are not in their hand.

Together with the soundness of his certainty that his affair is committed to the decrees of the Creator (exalted be He), and that the choice of the Creator for him is the most excellent choice — yet he is bound to the engagement with the causes of his welfares and to choose what is most excellent in the apparent state of the matter before him; the carrying-out of what has gone before by decree belongs to God (mighty and exalted).

Like this: the human, even if his term and the span of his life are reined-in by the decree of the Creator (exalted be He), it is incumbent upon the human to engage with the causes of life — using food, drink, clothing, and dwelling according to his need — and not to leave that to God, saying: "If it has gone before in God's decree that I shall live, He will preserve my soul in my body without nourishment throughout the span of my life, and I shall not burden myself with the toil of seeking sustenance and the wearying of myself in it." Likewise it is not fitting for him to expose himself to ruinous places out of reliance on the decree of God (exalted be He) — drinking poisons, risking himself in combat with lion and beast for no necessity, casting himself into the sea or into fire and the like, in things in which the human is not safe from destruction — and so risk himself. Scripture has prohibited us from this, in His saying: "You shall not test the Lord your God" (Deuteronomy 6:16).

For at that he is not free from one of two cases: either he perishes — and is the killer of himself, charged for that as for his killing of another rational being, even if his death by that aspect is by God's decree and permission. God has prohibited us from causing the killing of any rational being, in His saying: "You shall not murder" (Exodus 20:13). The closer the killed one is in relation to the killer, the more emphatic the punishment, as He said: "Because he pursued his brother with the sword and stifled his compassions" (Amos 1:11). So too the killer of himself: the most severe punishment and the most emphatic torment is incumbent upon him without fail. For his case in this is the case of a slave whose master has bound him to keep a certain place for a known span and prohibited him from moving from it until the messenger of his master comes to him; when the messenger is delayed, he moves on without his master's messenger coming to him — and his master is angered with him and binds the most severe punishment upon him. So too the one who kills himself: he has gone outside the obedience to God to the limit of disobedience to Him by exposing himself to the causes of perishing.

For this reason you see Samuel the Prophet (peace be upon him) saying to God (exalted be He), "How shall I go? Saul will hear and kill me" (1 Samuel 16:2) — and that was not reckoned to him as a deficiency in his reliance upon God; rather the answer came from God in such a way as to indicate that this was praiseworthy prudence on his part, as He said: "Take a heifer with you, and say: 'I have come to sacrifice to the Lord'" (1 Samuel 16:2), and the rest of the story. If this had been a falling-short in his reliance, the answer would have been to him: "I am the One who deals death and gives life," or the like — as He said to Moses (peace be upon him) when he said to Him: "I am heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue" (Exodus 4:10) — "Who has set a mouth in the human, or who makes one mute or deaf, or seeing or blind? Is it not I, the Lord?" (Exodus 4:11).

If Samuel, in the perfection of his bounty, did not see it as light to expose himself to the slightest cause of perishing — even though his exposing himself to that was by the command of the Creator (exalted be He), since He had said to him "Fill your horn with oil, and I shall send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite" (1 Samuel 16:1) — how much more rightful that this be ugly from someone other than him without a command from God to him. Otherwise: he is delivered by the protection of God (exalted be He), and his good deeds depart and his reward is destroyed, as the early ones said: "Let no man stand in a place of danger and say 'they will work a miracle for me,' for perhaps they will not work a miracle for him; and if they do work a miracle for him, it is deducted from his merits" (b. Shabbat 32a). And the Friend (peace be upon him) said: "I have become small from all the kindnesses and from all the truth that You have done with Your servant" (Genesis 32:11), and the people of the Targum translated: "*My merits have grown few from all the kindnesses and from all the goods*."

As is the discourse on life and death, so is the discourse on the obligation of engagement with the causes of health, food, clothing, dwelling, and goodness of traits, and the warding-off of their afflictions — together with the soundness of his certainty that the causes do not benefit him in this at all except by the decree of the Creator (exalted be He). Just as it is incumbent on the owner of land to plow it, clear it of thorns, sow it, and water it if water is possible to him — and to rely upon God (mighty and exalted) to make it grow, guard it from misfortunes, purify its yield, and grant blessing to him in it — and it is not incumbent upon him to leave the land without cultivation and sowing out of reliance upon God's decree that the earth would sprout without prior sowing.

So too the master of a craft, of commerce, and of hire is commanded to engage with the causes of sustenance by them, together with goodness of reliance upon God: that sustenance is in His hand and His judgment, and that He guarantees the human and delivers it to him by whatever cause He wills. Let him not suppose that the cause benefits him or harms him at all. If his sustenance comes to him by one of the aspects of the causes he engages with, it is fitting that he not be at home in that cause — that he not be charmed by it nor increase his clinging to it, so that his reliance on God grows weak and he inclines his heart toward it. Rather, let him not suppose that he profits by it more than what has gone before in the knowledge of God; let his clinging to it and his exposure to it not delight him; rather, let him thank God (exalted be He), who has sustained him after his striving and has not disappointed his weariness and his fatigue — as He said: "When you eat the labor of your hands, happy are you, and it is well with you" (Psalms 128:2). One of the righteous said: "I marvel at the one who gives to another what God has decreed for him with him, and then reproaches him for it and seeks thanks for it; and I marvel even more at the one who takes his sustenance at the hand of another, who is compelled to give it to him, and abases himself before him, exalts him, and thanks him."

If sustenance does not come to him by the aspect by which he sought it, then either his daily sustenance has come to him already and is in his possession, or it has come to him by another aspect; in either case, it is not fitting for him to abandon causes nor to slacken from engagement with them, when they are agreeable to his constitution, his body, his religion, and his this-world according to what has gone before. Let him rely upon God in this — that He is not heedless of him and does not neglect his affair — as He said: "Good is the Lord as a stronghold in the day of distress; He knows those who take refuge in Him" (Nahum 1:7).

So too the discourse on the matter of health and sicknesses: that it is incumbent on the human to rely upon God in this, and to strive in the perpetuating of health by the causes that have this in their nature, and the warding-off of sickness by what custom has run for warding it off — by what God (mighty and exalted) has commanded in His saying "and shall surely heal" (Exodus 21:19) — without relying on the causes of health and sickness as themselves benefiting him or harming him, except by the permission of God (exalted be He). When he relies on God, He heals him from his sickness, with cause or without cause, as He said: "He sends His word and heals them, and delivers them from their pits" (Psalms 107:20). Sometimes He heals him by the most harmful causes for him, as you have learned from the story of Elisha with the bad waters: in His saying, "And the waters were bad and the land bereaving" (2 Kings 2:19) — that he warded off their harm with salt. So too in His saying: "And the Lord showed him a tree, and he cast it into the waters and the waters became sweet" (Exodus 15:25) — and the early ones (may God be pleased with them) reported that it was the oleander tree. And like it: "Let them take a cake of figs and apply it to the boil, and he shall live" (Isaiah 38:21). You have learned what came in the story of Asa, when he relied upon physicians and abandoned reliance upon God in his sickness, of the rebuke against him; and Scripture said: "For He wounds and binds up" (Job 5:18).

As for the explication of the second division — namely, the matters of the human's earning and the causes of his sustenance and the modes of his employment in commerce, craftsmanship, travel, agency, hire, governance, the service of kings and their administration, contracting, deposit-keeping, scribal work, the various forms of service, hunting on land and sea, and the like — that which is used for the acquiring of wealth and the increasing of the surplus of livelihood:

The aspect of right reliance on God in this is that the human expose himself to what God has prepared for him of these for moderation, subsistence, and the taking of sufficiency from the world. If God has decreed for him an addition over that, He gives it to him without harshness or hardship, when he relies on God in it and is moderate in his exposure to the causes and does not lean upon them with his heart. If God has not decreed for him more than the subsistence — though the people of heaven and earth should aim at increase over it, this would not be possible for them in any aspect or by any cause. So when he relies upon God in this, he attains the rest of his heart, the repose of his soul, and the ease of his mind — for his sustenance does not pass beyond him to another, neither advances nor delays beyond its time decreed for him in it.

God may run abundant sustenances of His servants by the hand of one person of them, that he be tested by it as to his obedience or disobedience to God: He makes it among the strongest causes of trial and temptation upon him — like the king who sustains his army and his retinue, and likewise viziers, men of authority, and governance, in the shadow of whom live ranks of their attendants, servants, agents, slaves, dependents, and relations, who burden themselves on their account with engagement with the causes of earning by aspects of beauty and ugliness. The ignorant among them errs in three aspects.

**The first**: in his earning of wealth — for he takes what God has decreed for him to take by the ugliest aspects and the basest. If he had sought it by its [proper] aspect, he would have obtained it on the most desirable terms, the matter of his religion and his this-world would have been ordered for him, and nothing would have fallen short of what God had decreed for him.

**The second aspect**: that he reckons all that comes to him of wealth to be the sustenance of his nourishment, not realizing that sustenance is divided into three divisions. The first: the sustenance of his nourishment — the subsistence of his body alone — which is the guaranteed-from-God for every living being to the conclusion of his term. The second: the sustenance of the nourishment of others under him — dependents, children, attendants, retinue, and the like — which is not guaranteed by God (exalted be He) for all servants but for the elect of them, with specific conditions; this is an accident, made ready at one time and not another, according to what the currents of judgments from God in bounty and justice oblige. The third: the sustenance of property — namely, the wealth from which the human has no benefit, and upon him is its keeping and protecting, until he bequeaths it to another or it perishes from him. The ignorant reckons all that has been decreed for him of wealth to be the sustenance of his nourishment and the subsistence of his body, so he gulps after it and is eager for it; perhaps he gathers it for the husband of his wife after him, and his killer, and the bitterest enemy he has.

**The third aspect**: that he delivers the sustenances to their owners — what God has decreed for them through his hand — and reproaches them for it; he wishes to attract their thanks, to multiply their praise for it, and the rendering-of-service to him on its account. His soul grows haughty, conceit and self-glory enter him, and he turns away from thanks to God (exalted be He) for it. He has supposed that, were he to have withheld it from them, it would have remained with him; and that, were it not for him, their sustenances would have been cut off. He is the wretched one whose striving is disappointed in this world and whose reward is destroyed in the next. The intelligent runs in the three aspects according to what agrees with his religion and his this-world, his confidence in what is in the hand of God concerning his sustenance and his earning being stronger than his confidence in what is in his own hand of that — for he does not know whether it is sustenance of nourishment or sustenance of property; so he attains honor in this world and a beautiful end in the next, as it says in the psalm "Hallelujah, happy is the man who fears the Lord" to the end (Psalms 112).

There are ranks among people who do not labor in the earning of wealth and the multiplying of it except out of love of honor from people and the spreading of fame among them; nothing of it satisfies them — and that is from their ignorance of the causes of honor in this world and the next. What carries them to this is what they observe of the populace exalting the possessors of wealth and honoring them out of greed for what is with them and eagerness for the attracting of what is in their hands. If they were intelligent and certain that it is not in their power nor their capacity to deliver a single coin of it except to the one for whom God has decreed it with them — they would not hope in any but God (mighty and exalted), nor reckon as deserving honor with them any but the one whom God has singled out with praiseworthy excellences who is worthy of God's honor (exalted be He), as He said: "For those who honor Me I shall honor, and those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed" (1 Samuel 2:30). When the populace, in their honoring of the possessors of wealth, is ignorant of the causes of honor, this increases them in ignorance of the causes of what they seek; they fall into intense eagerness, exertion, and stratagem throughout their lives — heedless of what was more incumbent upon them of striving and eagerness in fulfilling the dues of God (exalted be He) toward Him and thanksgiving for His blessing toward them; and what they sought would have been closer to them by this path without fail, as He said: "Length of days is in her right hand; in her left, riches and honor" (Proverbs 3:16); and He said: "And wealth and honor come from before You, and You rule over all; and in Your hand are power and might; and in Your hand it is to make great and to strengthen all" (1 Chronicles 29:12).

In the totality of seekers of wealth, there is the one who reaches by it the limit of his hope through the path of the causes we have mentioned. There is the one who reaches it by the path of inheritance and the like — and supposes that the cause has necessitated this for him, and that without it nothing of it would have come to him; so he thanks the cause to the exclusion of the Causer. He resembles in this a human in a desert who, parched by thirst, finds non-sweet water settled in a cistern; he rejoices in it greatly and is satiated by it. He has gone only a little distance when he hits upon a flowing fountain — good and sweet — and grieves at his prior drinking of the first water and his being satiated from it. Likewise the possessor of wealth obtained by some cause: if that cause had become impossible to him, he would have attained it by another cause, according to what we have set down — as He said: "For there is no constraint with the Lord to save by many or by few" (1 Samuel 14:6).

Of what is fitting for the one who relies on God in his sustenance, when his sustenance is delayed from him on a given day: that he should say to himself, "He who brought me forth into this world at a specific time and a specific moment, and did not bring me forth before it or after it, is the One who withholds my sustenance from me until a known time and a known day, on account of His knowledge of what agrees with me." So too when measured sustenance comes to him with no surplus over his subsistence: it is fitting for him to think within himself and to say, "He who prepared my nourishment in the breast of my mother at the start of my affair according to my need and the measure of my subsistence — day by day — until He recompensed me for it with a more excellent than it, and the measured coming of it harmed me in nothing — likewise this sustenance, to which He has now moved me, measured according to my need to the conclusion of my term, harms me in nothing." He is rewarded for this, as God (exalted be He) said of our forebears in the wilderness, whose state this was, in the saying of Scripture: "And the people went out and gathered the matter of the day in its day" (Exodus 16:4); and He said: "Go and proclaim in the ears of Jerusalem, saying: I remember for you the kindness of your youth, the love of your espousals, your going after Me in the wilderness, in a land not sown" (Jeremiah 2:2).

So too if his sustenance comes to him by one cause and not another, in one place and not another, by the hand of one person and not another, let him say within himself: "He who created me with this form, this figure, this constitution, and this disposition, to the exclusion of the rest of figures, forms, and dispositions, for the rectitude of my state — He has chosen for me that my sustenance come by the aspect that agrees with my state and not the rest of aspects. He who brought me forth into this world in a specific place, by the hand of two specific persons and not the rest of the persons of the world, has chosen for me that my sustenance come in a specific land and by the hand of one whom He has made a cause for my sustenance, as a rectitude for me and a tender care toward me," as the Friend said: "Righteous is the Lord in all His ways" (Psalms 145:17).

As for the explication of the matters of the third division — namely, the affairs of his dependents, his children, his household, his clan, his friends, his enemies, his acquaintances, his confederates, and those above and below him among the ranks of people:

The aspect of right reliance on God in them is what I shall describe. Every human is not free from one of two cases: either a stranger, or one having household and relation. If he is a stranger, let him take comfort in God in his loneliness, let him rely upon Him in his state of estrangement, let him bring to mind the estrangement of the soul in this world — that the people of the earth are in the rank of strangers in it, as Scripture said: "For sojourners and dwellers are you with Me" (Leviticus 25:23). Let him think within himself that every possessor of relations soon returns a stranger and an isolated one — neither household nor child profits him, nor does any of them harvest him. Then let him think on the falling away from him of the great toil of them, their dues, and their incumbencies upon him; let him reckon that as a blessing from the blessings of God upon him. For if he is a seeker of the matters of this world and its requirements, his burden and his exertion would be easier upon him without dependents and children — so the absence of them is rest for him and care for him. If he is a seeker of the matters of his next world, his mind is more at ease and his heart more empty for that in his state of solitude, without fail. For this reason the people of asceticism in this world used to flee to the mountains, away from their household and their homelands, that their souls might be empty for obedience. So too the prophets, in the era of prophecy, would go out from their homelands and seclude themselves for the obligatory due of God upon them, as you have learned from the story of Elijah with Elisha — when He said of him: "And he was plowing with twelve yoke before him, and he was with the twelfth" (1 Kings 19:19); and when Elijah signaled to him with a subtle sign, he understood, and said to him: "Let me, I pray, kiss my father and my mother, and I shall come after you" (1 Kings 19:20); and He said: "And he went after Elijah and ministered to him" (1 Kings 19:21).

It has been said that one of the ascetics entered a city to guide its people to God (exalted be He). He found them clothing themselves in a single color in their dress and garment, and saw their tombs at the doorways of their houses — and he saw no woman among them. He asked them about this. They said to him: "We have clothed ourselves in a single color of garment, that the weak among us not be distinguished from the rich, that conceit and pride in his wealth not befall the rich, nor the weak grasp baseness and abasement from his self — so that our state above the dust resembles our state beneath it. It has been said of one of the princes that he used to mingle with his slaves so as not to be distinguished among them, in his aim at humility in his bearing and dress.
