We have set up the tombs of our dead at our doorways that we may take instruction from them and be on guard against death, that we may prepare for it the provision that delivers us to the house of stability. As for what you have seen of our withdrawing from women and offspring: we have set them apart in a village near us; when one of us needs anything from them, he goes up to them, takes care of his purpose, and turns back to us — for we have seen what enters in upon us of the preoccupation of mind and the great trial and the much burden and toil in their neighborhood; and the rest from this is in being far from them, in preference for the next world and asceticism in the matters of this world." The ascetic among them found this beautiful, prayed for them, and admiring-envied them in their state.

If the one who relies upon God is a possessor of household, kin, friends, and enemies — let him rely upon God for his safety from them; let him strive in fulfilling their dues and meeting their needs; let him purify his inner being toward them; let him hold his hand from harming them; let him seek the cause of what agrees with them; let him counsel them and guide them to the kinds of their welfares in religion and worldly life — out of obedience to God (exalted be He), as He said: "And you shall love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18); and He said: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart" (Leviticus 19:17). Not for recompense from them, nor for [building up] a store with them, nor for love of honor and praise from them, nor for seeking authority over them — but in obligation to the command of God and obedience to His covenant and His injunction concerning them. For whoever runs to anything of what we have first mentioned in meeting their needs does not attain his purpose from them in this world; his striving is disappointed and his reward destroyed in the next world. If he runs in this in obedience to God alone, God assists them in recompensing him in this world, looses their tongues with thanks of him, magnifies his affair in their hearts, and abundant reward accrues to him in the next world — like what God said to Solomon, "And also what you have not asked I shall give you, both wealth and honor" (1 Kings 3:13).
As for the aspect of his reliance on God in the affairs of those above him and below him among the ranks of people:

The aspect of right for him, when necessity calls him to seek a need from one above or below him, is to rely on God in this and to make them causes in its meeting — as he makes the cultivation of the earth and its sowing a cause for his sustenance. If God wills to sustain him from it, the seed sprouts, grows, and is purified — and the earth is not thanked in this; thanks belong to God alone. If God does not will to sustain him from it, the earth sprouts nothing, or sprouts and the growth meets a misfortune — and there is no blame upon the earth. So too when he requests a need of one of created beings: let the weak and the strong of them be alike with him in its meeting; let him rely on God for its completion. If it is met by the hand of one of them, let him praise God (mighty and exalted), who has met his need, and thank the one by whose hand it has been met for the goodness of his intent and his inner being toward him — for God has run his welfare upon his hands. It is well-attested that God (exalted be He) does not run welfare except upon the hands of the righteous, and seldom does corruption run upon their hands, as the early ones said: "*Merit is conducted by way of the meritorious, and culpability by way of the culpable*" (b. Shabbat 32a); and they said: "No iniquity shall come upon the righteous" (Proverbs 12:21). If his need is not met by their hands, they should not be blamed, nor any falling-short ascribed to them; rather let him thank God (exalted be He), who has chosen the better for him in this, and let him thank them in proportion to his knowledge of their eagerness and aim to meet his need — even if it has not been completed according to his desire and theirs. So too in his acquaintances and his friends, his commercial partners, his business contacts, and his associates.

So too if one above him or below him burdens him with the meeting of a need: let him cause himself to perform it by his intent, and expose himself to its meeting by his inner being if it is possible to him, and the one who has burdened him with its meeting is worthy of striving for him in it; then let him rely on God for its completion. If it is met by his hand, let him not thank himself for that, nor seek thanks or recompense from his companion for it; rather let him thank God (exalted be He), who has met it by his hand and made him a cause for the welfare of another. If it becomes impossible for him and he cannot meet it, let him not blame himself; let him excuse himself to his companion, after the giving of effort and life-blood in this.

As for the affairs of his enemies, his enviers, and those who hate him: let him rely upon God in their affairs, and bear with patience their offenses. Let him not requite them with the like of their actions; rather let him bestow bounty upon them and be beautiful with them in everything he can extend to them of beautiful conduct. Let him bring to mind, within himself, that his benefit and harm are in the hand of the Creator (exalted be He). If they have been a cause for harm to him, let him think well of them and ill of himself, of his actions, and of his evil prior matters before his Lord; let him repent to God and beseech Him for the forgiveness of his sins. Then his enemies will return to friendship with him, as the Wise One said: "When the Lord is pleased with the ways of a man, even his enemies He makes peaceful with him" (Proverbs 16:7).

As for the explication of the fourth division — namely, the affairs of the duties of the heart and the limbs whose benefit and harm are restricted to the human alone — this is like fasting, prayer, *sukkah*, *lulav*, *tzitzit*, the keeping of the Sabbath and the festivals, the desisting from the forbidden, and the totality of duties of the heart that do not pass beyond him to another, whose benefit and harm are restricted to him to the exclusion of the rest of people:

The aspect of right reliance in all of these on God (exalted be He) is what I am explicating — and God I ask to guide us to the truth by His mercy. The works of obedience and disobedience are not made valid from the human except by the gathering of three things: the one of them, the choice of obedience by his intent and his inner being to God (exalted be He); the second, the aim and resolve to carry out the act for which his choice has fallen upon it; the third, the engagement with carrying out the act by his outer limbs and its going forth to the bound of the act.

What is not hidden from us of these — namely, the choice of obedience and disobedience, and the aim and resolve upon the act — reliance upon God in this is error and ignorance, for God (exalted be He) has committed to us the choice of His obedience and His disobedience, as Scripture said: "And you shall choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:19). He has not committed to us the carrying-out of the work in obedience and disobedience except by causes outside of us — present at some times and impossible at others. Whoever relies on God for the choice of God's obedience, saying, "I shall not choose, nor aim at the doing of any work of God's obedience until He chooses for me what is in it of welfare for me from among them" — has erred from the path of guidance, and his two feet have slipped from the aspect of right. For God has commanded us to choose the working of obediences, to aim at them with diligence, resolve, and truthful intent — seeking His face (mighty and exalted); and He has informed us that this is the aspect of right for us in this world and the next. If the causes are made ready and the carrying-out of the work in obedience to God is possible — for which our choice has been previously made — abundant reward is made valid for us for the choosing of obedience, the resolve of working at it, and the carrying-out of its act by the outer limbs. If the carrying-out of its act becomes impossible for the limbs, the reward of the choice and the aim is made valid for us, according to what we have mentioned in what came before. So too the punishment for disobedience.

The difference between obedience and the rest of the works of this world in the matter of reliance on God (mighty and exalted) is this: as for the rest of the matters of this world, the aspect of welfare and good has not been disclosed to us in one cause to the exclusion of others, nor the aspect of corruption and evil in some of them to the exclusion of some. For we do not know which of the crafts is more right for us and more fitting for us in the seeking of sustenance, health, and good; nor in which of the commercial ventures, journeys, or worldly works we shall succeed when we engage with them. The duty incumbent upon us is to rely upon God in choosing them and carrying them out, that He may be a beautiful aid to us upon what is in our welfare after exposure to them; let us beseech Him to inspire in us the choice of the most right of them for us and the most fitting of them for us. As for obedience to God, it is not so — for He has acquainted us with the aspects of right in them and has commanded us to choose them after binding it upon us; so if we beseech Him in choosing them and rely upon Him in His showing-us the aspect of welfare among them, that would be error from our saying and ignorance from our reliance — since His showing-us the kinds of obedience that benefit us in this world and the next has already preceded, as Scripture said in the reward of this world: "And the Lord has commanded us to do all these statutes, for our good all the days" (Deuteronomy 6:24); and He said in the reward of the next world: "And it shall be a merit to us, if we are careful to do…" (Deuteronomy 6:25).

Furthermore: the affairs of this world — the praiseworthy cause may turn blameworthy and the blameworthy praiseworthy. As for obedience and disobedience, it is not so: their praiseworthy and blameworthy do not pass over from their state ever, nor are they exchanged. As for that in which it is fitting that we rely upon Him: it is the carrying-out of the works of obediences after choosing them with truthful intent, with resolve and diligence, with purity of inner being, with wholehearted devotion to His face (exalted be He). In this it is incumbent upon us to beseech God that He aid us in it and guide us to it — as the Friend said: "Lead me by Your truth and teach me" (Psalms 25:5); and he said: "Lead me in the path of Your commandments" (Psalms 119:35); and he said: "I have chosen the way of faithfulness" (Psalms 119:30); and he said: "I have clung to Your testimonies, O Lord; do not put me to shame" (Psalms 119:31); and he said: "Do not snatch the word of truth from my mouth utterly" (Psalms 119:43). All of this is evidence that his choice has fallen upon the working of obedience; but he is desirous from God in two matters. The first: the purification of his heart and the strengthening of his choice for obedience by the negating of the preoccupations of this world from his heart and his sight — that is his saying, "Make my heart undivided to fear Your name" (Psalms 86:11), and: "Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things from Your Law" (Psalms 119:18), and: "Pass my eyes from looking upon vanity" (Psalms 119:37), and: "Incline my heart to Your testimonies, do not incline my heart to an evil thing… redeem me from the oppression of man" (Psalms 119:36, 134), and what is like that. The second: the strengthening of his limbs upon carrying out the work in His obedience — that is his saying, "Lead me in the path of Your commandments" (Psalms 119:35), and: "Help me, that I may be saved, and that I may dwell upon Your statutes continually" (Psalms 119:117), and many like it. We shall return, in what we go on to, to the aspects of the corrupters of this division and the aspects of its completion and rightness, if God wills.

As for the explication of the fifth division — namely, the duties of the limbs whose benefit and harm pass from the human to another: like charity, the *zakāh*, the spreading of knowledge, commanding the right and forbidding the wrong, the rendering of trusts, the keeping of secrets, speaking the beautiful, doing the beautiful, righteousness toward parents, the guidance of the disobedient to God, the counseling of people in the aspects of their guidance, compassion upon their weak, mercy toward them, the bearing of their offenses when one calls their attention to obedience to God, and enticing them and warning them by promise and threat:

The aspect of right is reliance in this on God (exalted be He), and that the human intends all these works and the like, chooses their working and engages with them according to his capacity, in accordance with what has come before us in the fourth division of the obligation of choice upon us and its incumbency upon us — as a means of nearing to God only, not for praise and honor from them, not for recompense from them, not for advance through authority over them. Then let him rely upon God in the carrying-out of what he aimed at doing among them according to what He (exalted be He) is pleased with from him, after his beseeching of Him. Let him aim, in all of this, according to his capacity, at concealing his deed from one whom necessity does not call to be informed of it; for its being a secret is greater for his reward than its being open. What he cannot conceal, let him bring to mind the principle we have set down: that benefit and harm do not come from created beings except by the permission of the Creator (exalted be He). When God runs upon his hand a beautiful deed, let him think within himself that it is a favor from God upon him and a blessing He has bestowed upon him; let the praise of people for it not delight him, nor let him desire their honor on its account — leading him to conceit in his deed and corrupting his inner being and his aim at God; he would lose his deed and destroy his reward. We shall return to that in its proper gate, if God wills.
As for the explication of the sixth division — namely, the reward of this world and the next that he has deserved by good work in this world:

That is, reward is of two kinds. Reward in this world only; and reward in the next world only. He may deserve the two rewards on a single deed. The Messenger has not explicated the exposition of this in detail; rather the Creator has guaranteed the nation a summary reward upon a summary deed. He has not requited reward upon obediences in this world as He has done that in punishment for disobediences in this world — namely, His explication of the deeds whose doer is bound to *seqilah*, *serefah*, *hereg*, *henek*, *malqut*, *karet*, and the death-penalties; the double payment, the four-and-five-fold payment; the damages of *shor*, *bor*, *shen*, and *esh*; *noten mum ba-adam*; *sholaḥat yad bi-mevushav*; *motziʾ shem raʿ*; and the like.
As for the reward of the next world and its punishment, the Messenger has explicated nothing of it in His Book, for several aspects.

Among them: that the form of the soul without the body is unknown to us, let alone what gives it pleasure or pain in that state of reward and punishment. He has explicated this only to one who used to understand this concept, as God (exalted be He) said to Joshua son of Jehozadak: "And I shall give you ones who walk among these standing here" (Zechariah 3:7) — for this cannot be in a state of the soul's binding to its body; rather He pointed to what is after death, that the soul becomes in the form of the angels in its simplicity, fineness, and abandonment of the use of its body, when its actions in this world have been purified, illumined, and refined.

Among them: because the reward of the next world and its punishment was transmitted from the prophets among the populace, and known by intellect among the elect; so He abridged the mention of it in every book — as He has abridged much of the explications of the laws and the obligations, in reliance upon the [oral] transmission.

Among them: because the nation was in ignorance and slightness of perception such that this was not concealed from the Book. The Creator (exalted be He) walked the way of the compassionate father with his small son when he wishes to discipline him with gentleness and tenderness — as He said, "For Israel is a youth, and I love him" (Hosea 11:1). When the father, in the state of his son's childhood, aims to teach him the disciplines by which he may ascend to the high degrees that the child is ignorant of at that time — were his father to entice him with them and say to him, "Bear the burden of discipline and teaching that you may ascend by them to the degrees of the excellences," he would not bear that, nor be led to it by his ignorance of them. But when he promises him for that what would give him pleasure in the immediate — food, drink, clothing, and a glittering ride, and the like; and warns him with what would pain him in the immediate — hunger, nakedness, beating, and the like; and persuades him with what comforts him of sensible signs and clear truthful witnesses — he finds it easy to bear the burden of discipline and bears with patience its toil. When he reaches his maturity and his intellect grows strong, he discriminates the purpose intended in his disciplining; he aims at its aim, and reckons as small the pleasure he was running toward at the start of his affair — and that was tender care for him.

So too the Creator (exalted be He) enticed the nation and warned it by an immediate reward and punishment, knowing that, when the nation was set right for obedience, its ignorance of the reward of the next world and its punishment would be uncovered for it; it would aim at obedience for its sake and run to it. Likewise the discourse on what came in the Book of corporealization of the Creator (exalted be He).

Among them: that the reward of the next world is not deserved by anyone of people by the rectitude of his deed alone. Reward is deserved from God by two causes after the good deed. The one of them: the guiding of created beings to the obedience to God, and bearing them to good deed for God — as He said: "And those who lead the many to righteousness are like the stars forever and ever" (Daniel 12:3); and He said: "And to the reprovers it shall be pleasant, and upon them shall come the blessing of good" (Proverbs 24:25). When the reward of his setting-others-right is gathered for the one who exerts himself, along with the reward of his own rectitude, and the reward of his purification and his patience, he is worthy of the reward of the next world from God (exalted be He). The second cause: bounty from God (exalted be He), generosity and beneficence from Him — as He said: "And to You, O Lord, is kindness, for You requite each man according to his deed" (Psalms 62:13). The reason in this is that the deed of the human, even were it the like of the meadow of the sea in its number, would not fulfill a single blessing among the blessings of God upon him in this world. How much more if there are slips and heedlessnesses on his part! If a settling-of-accounts came from God in seeking the thanks of His blessing from the human, his deed would fall away from him, and the slightest blessing of God upon him would consume it. So whatever there is of God's reward (exalted be He) for him — he does not deserve it by the deserving of his deed; it is by God's bounty upon him. As for punishment in the two abodes, it is by an obligatory right and an incumbent debt upon the human; only that God's bounty upon him is comprehensive in the two abodes, as He said: "And to You, O Lord, is kindness" (Psalms 62:13), and: "And He is merciful, He pardons iniquity" (Psalms 78:38).

Among them: that the good deed is divided into two divisions. Of it is hidden — only God (exalted be He) is informed of it, like the duties of the heart and what is like them. Of it is manifest upon the limbs, not hidden from created beings — namely, the laws whose performance is manifest upon our limbs. The Creator (exalted be He) requites the manifest deed upon the limbs with manifest reward in this world, and requites the hidden inner deed with hidden reward — and that is the reward of the next world. For this reason the Friend described it with a wording that indicates this, in his saying: "How abundant is Your goodness which You have stored up for those who fear You; You have done for those who hope in You before the children of men" (Psalms 31:20). So too the current of punishment in the manifest and the hidden runs upon the current of reward. The evidence for this is that the Creator (exalted be He) has guaranteed the nation, upon the manifest obediences upon the limbs, a manifest, hastened reward in this world — and it is explicated in the section of "If you walk in My statutes" (Leviticus 26:3 ff.); and so He has guaranteed it, upon the manifest, well-known disobediences, a manifest, hastened punishment in this world — for upon the bulk of the nation is only what is manifest of deeds, not what is hidden, as Scripture said: "The hidden things belong to the Lord our God, but the revealed things belong to us and to our children" (Deuteronomy 29:28); and Scripture said: "And if the people of the land hide their eyes from that man… then I shall set My face against that man" (Leviticus 20:4–5). As for the inner obediences and the hidden disobediences, the judgment of their reward and punishment is to God in this world and the next; for this reason Scripture has abridged the explication of the reward of the next world.

Among them: that the reward and punishment mentioned in the Book — the Messenger has paired with the reward of this world and its punishment the people of this world; and when Joshua son of Jehozadak was in the world of the angels, it was said to him: "And I shall give you ones who walk among these standing here" (Zechariah 3:7) — for this is the way of enticement and warning: that there be a resemblance of the time and the place. Understand.

Among them: that the reward of the next world has as its end-point the singling-out by God and the drawing-near to His highest light, as He said: "And your righteousness shall walk before you" (Isaiah 58:8); and He said: "And the wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament" (Daniel 12:3); and He said: "To bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be enlightened with the light of life" (Job 33:30). It is reached only by one with whom God is pleased; and the satisfaction of God (exalted be He) is the root of the reward, as He said: "For there is a moment in His anger, life in His satisfaction" (Psalms 30:6). And He said in the section "If you walk in My statutes" intimations indicating the satisfaction from God — namely, His saying: "And My soul shall not abhor you" (Leviticus 26:11), "And I shall turn toward you and shall be your God, and you shall be My people" (Leviticus 26:9, 12); and He said: "And He shall love you and bless you and multiply you" (Deuteronomy 7:13).

Reliance upon God for what He has promised the righteous of the reward of this world and the next upon obedience — that He shall fulfill that for whoever has deserved it, and so too shall fulfill what He has guaranteed of punishment for whoever has deserved it — is incumbent upon the believer; and his confidence in God in this is from the perfection of faith in Him, as He said: "And he believed in the Lord, and He counted it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6); and the Friend said: "Were it not that I had believed I would see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living…" (Psalms 27:13). It is not fitting for him to rely upon the rectitude of his deed and so guarantee for himself the reward in this world and the next upon his deed; rather let him strive and exert himself and labor in it as thanks for the blessings of God successive upon him — not in hope of an inaugurated reward he is to deserve by his deed; rather let him rely upon the bounty of God in it, after his exertion in fulfilling the thanks of God (mighty and exalted) for the magnitude of His prior gifts to him, as the early ones said: "Do not be like the slaves who serve the master on condition of receiving a gift" (m. Avot 1:3). One of the righteous used to say: "No one reaches the reward of the next world by his deed at the close-examination of the reckoning, in what is incumbent upon him toward God (exalted be He) for the blessings He has bestowed upon him; rather by God's bounty upon him. So do not be deceived by your deeds." As the Friend said in this concept: "And to You, O Lord, is kindness, for You requite each man according to his deed" (Psalms 62:13).

As for the explication of the seventh division — namely, the bestowal of God's bounty upon His saints and His chosen ones in the abode of the next world, of abundant blessings whose description we cannot encompass:

The aspect of reliance upon God in this is the engagement with the causes that bring him to the degrees of the saints who deserve this from God (mighty and exalted) — namely, the assuming of the dispositions of the people of asceticism in this world, the bringing forth of the love of it and the preferring of it from his heart; the recompensing of that with love for God, the cutting-off to Him, and the taking comfort in Him; the becoming alienated from this world and its people; the conducting of himself in it after the way of the prophets and the chosen ones. Then let him think well of God (exalted be He): that He bestows bounty upon him as He bestowed upon them in the next world. As for the one who relies upon God to bring him to that without the means of work, he is the ignorant fool; he is in the rank of the one of whom the early ones (peace be upon them) mentioned: "*They do the deed of Zimri and seek the reward of Phinehas*" (b. Sotah 22b).

Of the marks of the people of this elevated degree are: the guidance of God's servants to the obedience of God; patience in trial and affliction; the slighting of every thing alongside the upholding of the command of God — as you have learned in the story of "And God tested Abraham" (Genesis 22:1), and the story of Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah in the fiery furnace, and the story of Daniel in the lions' den, and the Ten Slain by the Kingdom. Whoever prefers death in obedience to God over life in disobedience to Him, poverty over wealth, sickness over health, and affliction over wellbeing — out of surrender to the judgment of God and contentment with His decree — is worthy of the bounty of God upon him in the bliss of the next world, of which Scripture said: "To bequeath substance to those who love Me, and to fill their treasuries" (Proverbs 8:21); and He said: "Eye has not seen, O God, beside You, what He shall do for the one who waits for Him" (Isaiah 64:3); and He said: "How abundant is Your goodness which You have stored up for those who fear You" (Psalms 31:20).
As for the difference between the one who relies on God and another in the matter of engagement with the causes:
I say: the one who relies on God (exalted be He) is distinguished from the one who does not rely on Him in seven concepts.

**The first** — the one who relies on God is content with His judgment in all his states, and thanks Him in joy and adversity, as Job said: "The Lord has given and the Lord has taken; let the name of the Lord be blessed" (Job 1:21). The one who does not rely on God thanks himself in joy, as He said: "For the wicked has praised himself for the desire of his soul" (Psalms 10:3); and reproaches his Lord in adversity, as He said: "And it shall be, when he is hungry, that he shall be furious and curse his king and his God" (Isaiah 8:21).

**The second** — the one who relies on God is at rest of soul, calm of heart concerning the decrees, on account of his knowledge that they run from God in what agrees with him in his this-world and his next-world, as the Friend said: "But for God my soul waits in silence; for from Him is my hope" (Psalms 62:6). The one who does not rely on God is in continual anxiety, long worry, and a sadness that does not depart from him in his joy and his adversity — in joy, on account of the slightness of his contentment with his state and his greed for increase, ostentation, and accumulation; in adversity, on account of his despair at it and its contradiction of his desires and its opposition to his nature and traits. Of him the Wise One said: "All the days of the afflicted are evil" (Proverbs 15:15).

**The third** — the one who relies on God, even though he engages with the causes, does not lean upon them with his heart; he hopes from them no benefit and no harm apart from God's decree. He engages with them as a preference for the obedience to God who has commanded engagement in this world for its building-up and its adornment. If he attracts a benefit by them or wards off a harm, he praises God (mighty and exalted) alone for that, and he does not increase in admiring-envy of them nor in eagerness for them nor in repose toward them; rather his reliance upon God grows strong, and his heart is calmed toward Him to the exclusion of the causes. If he does not profit by the causes, he knows that his sustenance comes to him when God wills, from where He wills; this does not make him renounce them, nor abandon their use, in obedience to God (exalted be He). The non-reliant engages with the causes in reliance upon them, that they benefit him and ward off harm from him. If he profits by them, he thanks them, thanks his striving in them and his eagerness for them, and looks at nothing but them; if he does not profit by them, he disparages and despises them, and his eagerness turns from them — as Scripture said: "Therefore he sacrifices to his net and burns incense to his trawl-net, for by them his portion is fat and his food rich" (Habakkuk 1:16).

**The fourth** — the one who relies on God, when there is a surplus over his subsistence, disburses it in what agrees with the satisfaction of God (exalted be He) with openhandedness of soul and graciousness of heart, as the Friend said: "For from You is the all, and from Your hand we have given to You" (1 Chronicles 29:14). The non-reliant on God does not see the world with all that is in it as subsistence and provision sufficient for his need; so he excessively retains his wealth from delivering the dues of God and the dues of people from it; he does not perceive it until it perishes from him and he remains without it, as Scripture said of the two: "There is one who scatters and yet increases, and one who withholds more than is right, and it is only to want" (Proverbs 11:24).

**The fifth** — the one who relies on God exposes himself to the causes in this world only to provision himself with provision for the next world and a viaticum for his return. What is fit for him with the safety of his religion and his this-world, he engages in. What has in it a likelihood of corruption in his religion and an aim of disobedience to God, he does not expose himself to — lest he attract a sickness in place of medicine. The non-reliant on God is at home in the causes, his heart is calmed toward them, he avoids nothing of them, exposes himself both to the blameworthy and the praiseworthy, and gives no thought to the outcome of his affair, as the Wise One said of the two: "A wise man fears and turns from evil; but a fool throws off restraint and is confident" (Proverbs 14:16).

**The sixth** — the one who relies on God is a friend to all the ranks of people, and their souls take comfort in him on account of their safety from his harm and the safety of their hearts on his account: they do not fear him for their dependents and their wealth. He, too, is in safety from them, on account of his knowledge that his benefit and his harm are not in the hand of any created being nor in his power; he does not fear their harm just as he does not hope for their benefit. When he is in safety from them and they are in safety from him, they take him as a friend and he takes them as friends, as the Friend said: "And he who trusts in the Lord — kindness shall surround him" (Psalms 32:10). The non-reliant on God has neither friend nor compassionate one upon him; for he never ceases envying people and overstepping toward them. He reckons every blessing that has come to them as departed from him; that their sustenances are cut off from his sustenance; that whatever he is denied of his beloveds is from them; that in their hands is the bringing-of-his-hopes; if a misfortune or calamity reaches him in wealth or child, he supposes that this is from them, and to them is the lifting of harm and the warding-off of trial from him. When he has set up these premises in himself, there follows from him hatred of them, the calling-to-mind of their faults, the cursing of all of them, and enmity toward them; he is despised in the two abodes and cheated in the two stations, as the Wise One said: "The crooked of heart finds no good" (Proverbs 17:20).

**The seventh** — the one who relies on God is not saddened at the missing of a sought-after thing, nor at the loss of a beloved; he does not store up an existing thing, nor does he occupy himself with anything more than the sustenance of his day — for he does not speak with himself about what will come tomorrow, since he has no knowledge of when the conclusion of his term will be. He relies upon God for the extension of his span and the coming of his sustenance and his subsistence in it; he neither rejoices over what is to come nor grieves for it, as Scripture said: "Do not boast of tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may give birth to" (Proverbs 27:1); and Ben Sira said: "Do not be anxious over the trouble of tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may give birth to; tomorrow comes and he is not, and we are found troubling ourselves over a world that is not his." His worry and his sadness are only for his falling-short in what is incumbent upon him toward God of the dues; he exerts himself in fulfilling what he can of this with his outer and his inner — sensing death and the descent of fate. His fear of the descending of death upon him only adds to his emphasis and urging in provisioning himself for his next world and the slightness of his concern with preparing for this world. This is the saying of the early ones: "Repent one day before your death" (m. Avot 2:10) — and they expounded it: "Let him repent today, lest he die tomorrow; and he will be found all his days in repentance, as it is written, 'At all times let your garments be white'" (Ecclesiastes 9:8; b. Shabbat 153a).

The non-reliant on God is much-saddened by the succession of the world's misfortunes upon him: he loses his beloveds, his sought-after things slip from him, and he prepares much from the goods of the world — as if he had become safe from loss, and the fear of death had left him; as if his life would not pass away nor his term be completed and made finite. He becomes distracted from the next world and is preoccupied with this world, away from looking into the affairs of his religion, his provision, and his return. So his being-at-home in the prolongation of his term in this world is a cause of the lengthening of his hope in its affairs, and a cause of the shortening of his hope in his next world. When an admonisher admonishes him and a guide guides him, saying: "Until when will you be heedless of looking into your provision and the affairs of your return?" — he says: "When sufficiency and subsistence have been gathered for me and for all my household and dependents, until the conclusion of our matter, I shall calm my soul from the worries of the world, find leisure for fulfilling the dues of God, and look into the causes of provisioning for the day of return."

I see that I should make plain the aspects of their ignorance and error in this school in seven concepts, by which we shall uncover the magnitude of their ignorance and error — even if our discourse should grow long — for what is in this of rebuke and reproof to the people of this opinion, namely the people of pawned-pledges. For their reckoning in this is the reckoning of the merchant who, when he trades on credit with one who is not trusted with him, requires a pledge of him in his trading with him, out of fear of the slightness of his fulfilling and the slightness of his solvency and the impossibility of doing him justice.
The first aspect of the refutation upon him: I say —

O you who are in doubt about the decree of God, and uncertain about the splendor of the magnitude of God, the light of whose intellect has departed and the lamp of whose discernment has been extinguished by the overcoming of the darkness of his caprice upon him! Is it not the case that the seeking of a pledge and the taking of it from your adversary, your companion, who has no possession over you and whose command is not piercing in you — that is fitting from you; but as for the hireling, when he has hired himself out to one of people, it is not fitting from him to require a pledge from his employer for his wage before his service to him; and more rightful that the slave not require a pledge of his master before his service to him for his maintenance; and more rightful that the creature not require a pledge of his Creator before his obedience to Him? It is among the wonders that the slave's service to his master upon the condition of his being given his wage after his service is ugly — as in their saying, "Do not be like the slaves who serve the master on condition of receiving a gift" (m. Avot 1:3) — how then if he should be hardened and impudent in seeking a pledge for his maintenance before his service! Of his like Scripture said: "Do you so requite the Lord?" (Deuteronomy 32:6).

**The second aspect** — every receiver of a pledge from a pledger has a [definite] aim, and his sought-after has an end-point. As for the man of this opinion, his sought-after has no end-point; for he has no knowledge of what shall fulfill his maintenance and the maintenance of his dependents — of subsistence and surpluses — to the conclusion of their affair. Even if he attained of wealth manifold what would fulfill that, his soul would not be calmed; for their terms are unknown and the span of their lives unbounded. He is ignorant of the quantity of what he seeks, since it has no end-point with him and no measure.

**The third aspect** — the receiver of a pledge from his companion takes it only when an obligatory due has not preceded for him upon him, nor a binding debt been upon him for him; in that case, his excuse is plain. But when obligatory dues have preceded for his companion upon him, and known binding debts toward him, there is no aspect for the seeking of a pledge from him; nor is taking it from him permissible, even were the would-be pledge-holder to volunteer it. How much more the Creator (exalted be He), with whom the human has obligatory dues such that, were the deed of every rational being throughout the duration of the world to be gathered for one of people, the totality would not fulfill the right of one blessing among the blessings of God upon him! How then does this brazen-faced one not blush — to seek to advance against the Creator (exalted be He) abundant blessings beyond what has come before, so that the duty grows heavy upon him; and perhaps he does not fulfill what he has promised of obedience to God on account of the cutting-off of his term and the conclusion of the span of his life!

One of the righteous used to say to people: "O company of people: is it permissible that God (mighty and exalted) demand of you the obligations of tomorrow on this day of yours? — and so what is incumbent upon you in what is after it, for a year and years?" They said to him: "How is it permissible that we be demanded for the obligations of a span we do not know that we shall live to reach, that they be incumbent upon us? Obedience is incumbent upon us only as an imposed obligation in a bounded span; when we reach the span, obedience is incumbent upon us." He said to them: "So too the Creator (exalted be He) has guaranteed for you, for every bounded span, a known sustenance, in which obedience is imposed as an obligation upon you. As He does not demand of you obedience before its time, so it is fitting that there be in your faces a shame that prevents you from seeking sustenance whose time has not yet come. What ails you that I see you seeking from Him sustenances of years to come, of which you have no knowledge that your span will reach to them — and seeking in advance the sustenances of household and dependents not yet created; and not being content with subsistence alone, but seeking-in-advance the subsistence and the surpluses for an unknown span and unbounded days, not guaranteed for you? It is not enough for you that you do not advance for God an obedience for a forthcoming span — but you do not even reckon-with-yourselves for what you have neglected of obedience in days past, in which He did not neglect to deliver your sustenances to you."

**The fourth aspect** — every demander of a pledge from his companion demands it only for one of three reasons. The first: his poverty and slight means. The second: his stinginess with what he has, so that doing him justice is hard. The third: his fear of him on account of death. The pledge is the medicine for the like of these illnesses among people. If people were safe from one another from these three faults, the seeking-of-pledges from one another would be ugly without fail. So the Creator (exalted be He), to whom none of these descriptions is fitting, is more ugly by far and more outrageous to be pledged. Scripture has said: "Mine is the silver and Mine is the gold, says the Lord of hosts" (Haggai 2:8); and He said: "And wealth and honor come from before You" (1 Chronicles 29:12).

**The fifth aspect** — the receiver of a pledge from his companion: his soul is calmed by the pledge, since he hopes to do himself justice from him and to profit by it or by its substitute. As for the one who claims that, when God has advanced sufficiency to him, his soul will be calmed from the side of the world — his claim is a lie; for the remaining of the wealth with him is not guaranteed: it is possible that … […] obstructing misfortunes intervene against it, as Scripture said: "In the midst of his days he shall leave it, and in his end he shall be a fool" (Jeremiah 17:11). So what they have claimed of the calming of their souls upon the acquiring of their hope from the goods of the world is a lie and an ignorance of what they seek; perhaps it is a strong cause of the preoccupation of their mind and the agitation of their souls, as the early ones said: "Whoever multiplies possessions multiplies anxiety" (m. Avot 2:7).

**The sixth aspect** — the taker of a pledge from his companion, … […] it is sound from him that he do him justice before the falling due of his term, and recompense him for his patience with manifold what is due to him as a bounty upon him — would not pledge him by any aspect or for any cause. The Creator (exalted be He), who has acquainted us with the goodness of His excellences upon us and the beauty of His blessings to us, of old and recent, and that He requites the good deeds and the works of obediences with what cannot be conceived, let alone described — as Scripture said, "Eye has not seen, O God, beside You, what He shall do for the one who waits for Him" (Isaiah 64:3) — is more ugly by far that we should pledge Him.

**The seventh aspect** — he who pledges his companion pledges him only after the capacity to deliver what he is pledged for of the goods of the world. As for the one who would pledge the Creator (exalted be He) by the priority of His blessing toward him: he is one not fulfilling in the rendering of obedience to God in return for it; nor is he guaranteed in the upholding of the prior dues of God upon him, let alone the recent ones. The righteous slave does not fulfill the due of God's blessing upon him except by God's aid to him — as one of the excellent ones said in his praising of God (mighty and exalted): "*And the discerning one who knows You shall not glory in his deed, but in Your name and Your mercies — that You have prepared his heart to know You; for in You shall the seed of Israel be justified and glory, saying: 'In God we have praised all the day, and Your name forever…'*"
Now that we have given this gate its due in discourse according to our perception, it is fitting that we make plain the corrupters of reliance on God.
I say: the corrupters of the three preceding gates of this book are all of them corrupters of reliance on God.

Among its corrupters, also: ignorance of God (exalted be He) and of His beautiful attributes. For whoever is ignorant of God's mercy upon His creatures, His sufficiency for them, His attentiveness to them, His sovereignty and reining over them — his heart is not calmed toward Him, nor does he lean upon Him.

Among them: his ignorance of the command of God — I mean His Law, in which He has urged toward calm-toward-Him and reliance upon Him — as He said: "And try Me now in this" (Malachi 3:10), and: "Trust in the Lord forever and ever" (Isaiah 26:4).

Among them: his inclining toward the proximate causes that he handles. He is ignorant that the closer the causes are to the caused, the lesser their power to benefit the caused or to harm it; the further they are, the more their power to benefit and harm it is piercing and manifest. Like the prince, when he wills the punishment of one of his slaves, he commands his chamberlain to carry that out; the chamberlain commands the vizier; the vizier commands the chief of the police; the chief of the police commands his deputy; the deputy commands the constables; the constables take that up with instruments prepared for it. The weakest of them in power to lighten the pain or to strengthen it are the instruments, since they have no choice; then the constables are more powerful for that than the instruments; the deputy is more powerful than the constables; the chief of the police more powerful than the deputy; the vizier more powerful than the chief of the police; the chamberlain more powerful than the vizier; the prince more powerful than them all — for if he wills, he pardons him. It is plain that the weakness of the causes and their strength in their bringing of effect upon the caused are in proportion to their nearness and their distance from it. The Creator (exalted be He), who is the utmost of the causes in remoteness from caused things, is worthy of confidence in Him and reliance upon Him, on account of the piercing of His power for benefit and harm to them — as has come before us in the discourse.

The summary discourse on reliance: that the differential excellence of reliance among those who rely on God is in proportion to the differential excellence of their knowledge of Him and their certainty of His sufficiency for them and the strength of His attentiveness to what agrees with them. The infant at the start of his affair relies upon his mother's breast, as he said: "I have made me trust upon the breasts of my mother" (Psalms 22:10). When his discrimination grows strong, he turns reliance to his mother, on account of his knowledge of the intensity of her care for him, as he said: "If I have not stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child upon its mother" (Psalms 131:2). When his discrimination grows strong and he sees that the management of his mother is to his father, he turns his reliance upon him, on account of his fuller sufficiency for him. When his body grows strong and contrivance becomes possible to him in his livelihood — by craft, commerce, and the like — he turns his reliance upon his strength and his contrivance, in his ignorance of what has come before of God's beautiful management of him.

It has been said that one of the righteous had a neighbor who was a copyist, an excellent workman, who lived from the wage of writing. He said to him one day, "How is your state?" The copyist said, "I am well, so long as my hand is sound." That very evening his hand was paralyzed, and he did not write with it for the rest of his life — and that was a punishment from God for his reliance on his hand.

If his sustenance is made ready for him by the hand of others among created beings, he turns his reliance upon them and his soul reposes toward them. When his discrimination grows strong and he sees their poverty and their need of the Creator (exalted be He), he turns his reliance to Him and his leaning upon Him in the matters in which he has no contrivance and no sufficiency apart from Him for surrendering to the decree of God in them — like the descent of rains upon the seed-crop, travel by sea, the crossing of trackless wastes without water, at the onset of floods, at the falling of plagues among animals, and the like, in matters in which there is no contrivance for the human in any aspect, as Scripture said: "And in the time of their evil they shall say, 'Arise and save us'" (Jeremiah 2:27).

If his discrimination of God (exalted be He) grows strong, he relies upon Him also in what is possible to him of some contrivance — like the attracting of sustenance by feared causes and crafts wearying to bodies; he abandons them in reliance upon God that He sustains him by what is easy to use of them.

If his discrimination of God (mighty and exalted) grows strong, he turns his reliance to God in the totality of the causes — what is hard of them and what is easy — and his aim, in his exposure to them, is obedience to God and submission to His command.

If his discrimination grows strong more than that, by the gentleness of the Creator (exalted be He) toward His created beings, he is content with what comes of God's decree for him and upon him — with his heart, his tongue, his outer and his inner. He is delighted with everything God deals with him: death and life, poverty and wealth, health and sickness. He longs for nothing other than what God has chosen for him, nor wills anything but what God wills for him. He surrenders to God and casts himself and his body upon His judgment; he prefers no state over another, nor chooses anything other than what he is upon of the affairs of his this-world — as one of the reliant ones used to say: "I have never woken in a state and wished for any other."

If his discrimination of God grows strong more than that, and he knows the purpose for which he was aimed at by his being created and by his being brought forth into this perishing abode — and discriminates the excellence of the other, abiding abode — he renounces this world and its causes; he is severed, in his imagination, his soul, and his body, to God (mighty and exalted). He takes comfort in His remembrance in solitudes; he is alienated apart from thinking on His majesty. If he is in assemblies, he wishes only for His satisfaction, and longs only for the meeting with Him; his joy in His love preoccupies him from the joy of the people of this world in this world, and the joy of the people of the next world in the next world. That is the highest of the degrees of the reliant — among the prophets, the saints, and the elect of God, the chosen ones — as Scripture said: "Even in the way of Your judgments, O Lord, we have hoped for You; for Your name and for Your remembrance is the desire of the soul" (Isaiah 26:8); and the Friend said: "My soul has thirsted for God, for the living God" (Psalms 42:3).
These are the ten degrees of reliance, none of the reliant being free from one of them.

We have found the meaning of reliance in the Book of God expressed in the Hebrew tongue by ten words, in correspondence with these ten degrees: *mivṭaḥ*, *mishʿan*, *tiqvah*, *maḥseh*, *toḥelet*, *ḥikkui*, *semikhah*, *seber*, *misʿad*, *kesel*.
May God set us and you among those who rely upon Him, who surrender to His judgment in outer and inner — by His mercy (exalted be He).
